Google Business Profile: Getting the Basics Right for a Birmingham Small Business

Your Google Business Profile is often the first thing a local customer sees. Here are the rules Google actually sets for names, addresses, hours and reviews, and the simple habits that keep a profile accurate.

By Gibson Nyendwa · 4 November 2026 · 3 min read

On this page

  1. Use your real business name, and nothing else
  2. Your address: real premises or a service area
  3. Hours, categories, phone and website
  4. Reviews: ask fairly, reply well
  5. Keep your details the same everywhere
  6. A five-minute monthly check

When someone in Birmingham searches for a plumber, a hairdresser or a café near them, the first thing they often see is not a website. It is a Google Business Profile: the panel with your name, opening hours, phone number, photos and reviews.

Since 2016, much of my work through Gibcom has been helping small businesses get found online, and the profile is usually where I start. This guide sets out the rules Google publishes, which are stricter than many owners realise, and the habits that keep a profile working for you.

Use your real business name, and nothing else

Google asks you to use the name customers already know from your shopfront, website and stationery. Adding extra words, such as a service, a location or a slogan, is not allowed. Google's guidelines say plainly that including unnecessary information in your business name isn't permitted.

It is tempting to add "Birmingham" or "Emergency" to stand out. Don't. It breaks the rules, and profiles that break them can be suspended.

Your address: real premises or a service area

Google wants a real, physical location. A PO box or a remote mailbox is not acceptable, and a virtual office, where you rent a mailing address but do not work from it, is not eligible for a profile.

If you travel to customers, such as a mobile mechanic or a cleaner, you are a service-area business. You should have one profile for your base, with the areas you cover set as a service area, rather than separate profiles for every postcode you visit.

Hours, categories, phone and website

  • Hours: show your regular customer-facing hours and add special hours for bank holidays and Christmas. If you close for a season, mark the profile as temporarily closed rather than leaving old hours up.
  • Categories: choose the fewest that describe what your business is, as specifically as possible. Categories describe the business, not every service you offer.
  • Phone: use a number you control that connects to your business directly. Premium-rate numbers are not allowed.
  • Website: link to your own site, ideally the page for that location, without redirects.

Reviews: ask fairly, reply well

Reviews matter to customers and Google encourages you to ask for them, for example by sharing a link or QR code. There are firm limits, though. Google's policy says businesses must not offer payment, discounts or free goods or services in exchange for a review, or for changing or removing one. You also must not discourage negative reviews or ask only your happiest customers.

Replies are public, so keep them short, professional and specific. For a negative review, protect the customer's privacy, apologise where it is right to, and reply promptly. A calm, helpful reply is often read by more people than the original complaint.

Keep your details the same everywhere

My view is that consistency is underrated. If your name, address and phone number appear the same way on your profile, your website and local directories, customers are less likely to be confused and you are less likely to have out-of-date details floating around. It is one reason I started Birmingham Local Biz Support in 2021, a free directory for West Midlands businesses.

A five-minute monthly check

  • Are your hours right, including any holiday changes coming up?
  • Does the phone number ring through, and does the website link work?
  • Have you replied to every new review?
  • Are your photos current: the shopfront, the team at work, the products?
  • Has anyone suggested an edit to your profile that you need to accept or reject?
